part_title: Preparing and Evaluating ML Data — Splits, Features and Leakage
review_basis: Original numbered AIF module 03 WebP slides 22, 23 and 24 individually inspected: train/validation/test sets, feature engineering and target/data leakage house-price example.

scenes.title: Training vs. Validation vs. Test Set
scenes.narration: The slide begins with one labeled dataset at the top, shown as a collection of animal photographs. Follow the three arrows downward. We divide the data into separate groups because a model can appear excellent on examples it has already memorized while performing poorly on new information. The left group is the training set. It is used to learn patterns and fit model parameters. The picture uses dog and other animal images as examples. The slide gives a commonly seen proportion of sixty to eighty percent, but this is only a typical illustration, not a universal rule. The middle group is the validation set, represented by a stack beginning with a cat image. Validation examples help us tune the model and compare settings during development. For instance, we might compare two models and pick the one with better validation performance. The example allocation shown is ten to twenty percent. The right group is the test set, represented by a bird photograph. It is reserved for assessing the final model on unseen examples, with another illustrative ten to twenty percent. Why should we keep this last group separate? Imagine practicing with the same sample exam questions every day. A perfect score on those samples might reflect memorization, not broad understanding. The final exam is a better test of what you learned. In machine learning, repeated tuning against the test results can contaminate that assessment. The slide warns against this kind of data leakage and overly optimistic estimates. A practical safeguard is to split related records carefully, such as keeping photographs of the same animal or records of the same customer from leaking across groups where appropriate. For time-based predictions, a chronological split may be more realistic than random mixing. Read the bottom takeaway: use the training set to learn, validation to guide model choices, and the test set to estimate final generalization. Check your understanding. If a developer tries ten different settings and repeatedly selects the best using the test set, is that a trustworthy final test? No. Those test results have influenced development. Keep an untouched evaluation set for a fairer estimate.

scenes.title: Feature Engineering
scenes.narration: Feature engineering means turning raw information into inputs that are more useful for machine learning. Start on the left with four ideas. First, create useful features using knowledge of the problem. Second, select relevant features instead of automatically passing every available column. Third, transform features into a format the algorithm can use, for example by scaling numerical values or encoding categories. Finally, remember that thoughtful inputs often make it easier for supervised models to learn patterns that work on new examples. Follow the central diagram from raw data on the left to engineered features on the right. The raw customer table contains customer ID, name, birth date and purchase amount. A customer ID identifies a record, but that alone does not necessarily tell us whether the customer will stop buying. A date of birth can be transformed into an age at an appropriate observation date. In the illustration, Alice, Bob and Chen have engineered ages of thirty, forty-five and thirty-nine, alongside purchase amounts of two hundred, three hundred and one hundred twenty dollars. These are illustrative values; the precise calculation should depend on the relevant observation date. On the right, age and purchase behavior are suggested useful attributes, not a guarantee that these are the correct or legally appropriate inputs in every application. Under the gear, read the three techniques in sequence. Feature extraction derives new information; feature selection keeps the most relevant attributes; feature transformation changes representation, such as scaling a value or turning a category into numbers. The everyday example concerns customer churn, which means a customer stops using a product or service. A feature like age may be more meaningful than an unprocessed birth date for some models, but privacy, fairness and relevance still matter. Ask yourself: should every column in the database automatically become a model feature? No. A column may be irrelevant, sensitive, misleading or unavailable when making a real prediction. Good feature engineering starts with the actual question the model must answer.

scenes.title: Feature engineering without target leakage
scenes.narration: This slide takes the same idea into a five-step house-price workflow and highlights a dangerous mistake. Begin with step one. We know a property's floor area is two thousand four hundred, its location is Seattle, it has four bedrooms, and its build year is two thousand five. The example training record also has a known target sale price of eight hundred thousand dollars. Target means the answer we want the model to predict. That answer must stay separate from the model's input columns. Step two creates property age from the observation year, two thousand twenty-five, minus the build year, two thousand five, giving twenty years. Notice why the observation date matters: a property ages over time, so we must calculate its age as of the moment for which the prediction is intended. Step three keeps floor area, location, bedrooms and derived property age, and removes the older build-year column in this illustrative design. Step four transforms the inputs. The slide mentions standardizing floor area with a z-score and converting the location Seattle into a one-hot encoding, a list of indicator values such as zero, zero, one, zero. These are ways to represent input information in a useful numerical form. Step five passes prepared features into the trained model, which produces an illustrative predicted sale price of seven hundred eighty thousand dollars. Now look at the red warning beneath the workflow. Do not calculate price per square foot using the unknown sale price and then feed that value into the model. That would secretly give the model information derived from the answer it is supposed to predict. This is called target leakage. The comparison with the known sale price of eight hundred thousand dollars is appropriate during evaluation, but that known answer is not available for an actual new home's prediction. The lower right provides a second protection: fit preprocessing operations, such as scaling parameters and category mappings, on the training data only; apply those same fitted operations to validation and test data without refitting them there. This helps prevent evaluation information from influencing the training process. The evaluation box names MAE, RMSE and R squared as regression metrics. They compare predictions with real outcomes in different ways and will need correct interpretation rather than being treated as guarantees. Final decision check. Can we use a home's sale price to calculate an input for predicting that very sale price? No, because it leaks the answer. Can we use the build year and an observation date known when the prediction is made? Yes, if both are genuinely available and the derived feature is appropriate.
